summary: A humorous April 1st RFC defining Concat notation, a text-based language for describing pictures and videos involving cats and containers. It is a joke, not a real specification.

eli5.summary: A joke document about a made-up way to write down pictures of cats sitting in boxes.

questions: how to describe cats in boxes
subtitle: A text notation for describing cat pictures and container interactions.

tldr.problem: There is no compact text-based way to describe the position and interaction of cats, containers, and related subjects in pictures and videos.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9402 defines Concat notation, a grammar-based language using ASCII symbols. Cats are represented by the word 'cat' or partial letters (c, a, t). Containers are denoted by bracket types: square brackets for boxes, parentheses for round openings, and curly braces for soft containers. Operators specify position: + for horizontal adjacency, / for vertical stacking.
tldr.outcome: This April Fools' RFC creates a surprising amount of technical detail to standardize what is essentially internet cat content, using proper ABNF grammar and formal semantics.

today: RFC 9402 is an Informational RFC published on April 1, 2023. It remains the formal specification for Concat notation, though it has not been widely deployed for actual cat picture annotation.

sections.title: Describing Cat Pictures
sections.content: RFC 9402 is an April Fools' RFC that defines Concat notation, a text-based language for describing pictures and videos whose subject includes cats, containers, and their interactions. The document notes that cat pictures and videos are frequently shared across the Internet, and many display feline subjects interacting with boxes and containers. Since no compact notation previously existed, Concat provides a standard way to describe the position and interaction of cats and their surroundings using only US-ASCII characters, allowing transmission in restricted environments.
sections.eli5: Cats in boxes are popular on the internet. This joke invents a serious technical language to describe them in text.

sections.title: The Notation Grammar and Elements
sections.content: Concat uses a formal ABNF grammar to describe layouts. A cat is represented by the word 'cat' or, when partially hidden inside a container, by partial letters: c (head), a (body), t (tail), ca (head and body), or at (body and tail). Other animals use suitable descriptive words. Balls of yarn are represented by @. Containers are denoted by bracket types: square brackets [] for boxes, parentheses () for round openings, curly braces {} for soft containers, and angle brackets <> for grouping without containers. The + operator represents horizontal adjacency, and / represents vertical positioning when an object is above or on top of another.
sections.eli5: The notation uses symbols: 'cat' for a whole cat, 'c' for the head, 'a' for the body, 't' for the tail. Brackets show what type of container: [cat] is a cat in a box, (cat) is a cat in a round container.

sections.title: Positioning and State Changes
sections.content: Multiple objects are described left to right. Repeated objects use a shorthand: 3*[cat] means three cats in boxes side by side, while 2/[cat] means two cats stacked vertically. Videos and animations use the state change operator => to mark significant changes. For example, cat => [cat] describes a cat transforming into a cat inside a container. When multiple specific cats appear in a sequence, disambiguation identifiers distinguish them: cat1 and cat2. The RFC includes security considerations noting that cats may chew cardboard boxes and recommending multiple boxes as a mitigation strategy.
sections.eli5: To show multiple cats in a row, write 3*[cat]. To stack them vertically, write 2/[cat]. The arrow => shows when things change over time, like a cat entering a box.
